title: Comparable Companies Analysis (Trading Comps)
prompt: Value a mid-cap company using comparable companies analysis. Walk me through selecting the peer set, choosing and calculating the right multiples, normalizing them, and applying them to the target — then reconcile the result with an intrinsic method.
blurb: A relative-valuation interview — build a trading-comps analysis: pick a defensible peer set, choose EV/EBITDA vs P/E, calculate and normalize multiples, adjust for growth and margins, and apply to the target.

rubric.label: Comps framework
rubric.description: Lays out the full comps sequence: define the target, screen a peer set on the right criteria, choose appropriate multiples, calculate them consistently, normalize for one-offs, pick a central tendency (median), and apply to the target's operating metric to imply a value — in the right order.

rubric.label: Peer selection
rubric.description: Screens comps on business model, sector, size, growth, margins, and geography rather than just SIC code; explains why each name is in or out and recognizes that a tight, truly-comparable set of five is better than a loose set of twenty.

rubric.label: Multiple mechanics
rubric.description: Chooses EV/EBITDA vs P/E vs EV/Revenue with a reason, computes EV correctly (market cap + debt + preferred + minorities - cash), matches numerator to denominator (equity multiples to equity metrics, EV multiples to pre-financing metrics), and uses forward vs trailing consistently on a diluted, treasury-stock-method share count.

rubric.label: Normalization & adjustments
rubric.description: Strips out non-recurring items, stock-comp and lease distortions, and calendarizes to a common period; explains why a peer trades at a premium/discount (growth, margin, returns on capital) and adjusts rather than blindly applying the mean.

rubric.label: Judgment & reconciliation
rubric.description: Uses the median not the mean, presents a range not a point, sanity-checks the implied value against a DCF and precedent transactions, and articulates that comps capture current market sentiment whereas a DCF captures intrinsic value.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Explains each step clearly and in order, defines terms, and reasons out loud about why multiples differ rather than reciting a mechanical recipe.

reference.scenario: Conceptual + numeric trading-comps walkthrough for a mid-cap company — say a specialty-industrials or branded consumer business. The interviewer probes each step and may hand the candidate round numbers to test the mechanics, e.g.: the target has EBITDA of $200M and net debt of $300M; a screened peer set trades at a median forward EV/EBITDA of ~9.0x (range 7.5x-11x). Applying 9.0x implies enterprise value of $1,800M; subtract net debt for equity value of $1,500M, divide by shares for per-share. The interviewer will test whether the candidate can compute enterprise value correctly, match numerator to denominator, normalize a distorted peer multiple (e.g. a peer with a one-time gain or a much higher growth rate), justify using the median over the mean, and explain the choice of EV/EBITDA over P/E for a set with different capital structures. Exact figures matter less than defensible peer selection, correct multiple mechanics, thoughtful normalization, and knowing that comps give a market-sentiment range that should be triangulated against an intrinsic DCF.
model_points: State the goal: comps value the target relative to how the market currently prices similar public businesses, giving a range of implied values from peer multiples rather than an intrinsic estimate.

Screen the peer set on business model, industry, size, growth profile, margins, and geography — not just industry code. Justify each inclusion/exclusion; a tight set of five genuine comps beats twenty loose ones.

Choose the multiple with a reason: EV/EBITDA is capital-structure-neutral and strips D&A differences (good when leverage varies); P/E reflects the equity story but is distorted by capital structure and tax; EV/Revenue for unprofitable or early-stage names; sector-specific multiples (EV/EBITDAR, EV/subscribers) where relevant.

Compute enterprise value correctly: market cap (diluted shares via treasury-stock method x price) + total debt + preferred + minority interest - cash and equivalents. This is the bridge candidates most often get wrong.

Match numerator to denominator: EV multiples pair with pre-financing, pre-tax metrics (EBITDA, EBIT, revenue); equity multiples (P/E, P/B) pair with equity metrics (net income, book value). Never put net income under EV.

Use forward multiples where available (they reflect expected performance) and be consistent trailing-vs-forward across the set; calendarize peers to a common fiscal period so you compare like with like.

Normalize the metrics and the multiples: strip non-recurring items (restructuring, one-time gains/losses, litigation), adjust for stock-based comp and lease-accounting differences, and exclude or flag outliers driven by M&A rumors or distressed pricing.

Choose a central tendency — median over mean because the mean is skewed by outliers — and understand the dispersion: a peer trades at a premium usually because of higher growth, higher margins, or better returns on capital, so adjust the applied multiple toward the target's profile rather than blindly using the group median.

Apply the chosen multiple to the target's (normalized, forward) metric to get enterprise value, then bridge EV - net debt (- preferred - minorities) = equity value, / diluted shares = value per share; present a range from the multiple range, not a single point.

Reconcile with intrinsic and transaction methods: comps reflect current market sentiment and can be collectively over- or under-valued; cross-check against a DCF and precedent-transaction multiples (which include a control premium), and explain the differences.

probes.trigger: candidate screens peers only by industry/SIC code
probes.question: You've got everyone in the sector in your set — how do you actually decide who's a true comp? What makes a company comparable beyond being in the same industry?

probes.trigger: candidate can't justify EV/EBITDA vs P/E
probes.question: Why EV/EBITDA here rather than P/E? What does each multiple control for, and when would P/E mislead you across this peer set?
Walk me through building enterprise value from market cap precisely — what gets added, what gets subtracted, and why does cash come off?

probes.trigger: candidate puts net income under EV or mismatches metrics
probes.question: You've paired that multiple with that metric — is the numerator and denominator consistent? Which claimants does each one belong to?

probes.trigger: candidate applies the group mean without adjustment
probes.question: One peer trades at 11x and the target grows slower with thinner margins — do you still apply the group average? How do you adjust for growth and margin differences?
One comp had a big one-time gain in EBITDA this year — what does that do to its multiple, and how do you normalize it before including it?

probes.trigger: candidate gives a single point value and stops
probes.question: You've got an implied value from comps — how does it compare to what a DCF would say, and why might the two disagree?

red_flags: Selects peers by industry code alone with no screen on size, growth, margins, or business model
Computes enterprise value wrong — forgets to add debt/minorities or subtract cash, or uses basic instead of diluted shares
Mismatches numerator and denominator, e.g. puts net income or EPS under enterprise value
Can't articulate why EV/EBITDA is capital-structure-neutral or when P/E is distorted
Blindly applies the mean, ignoring outliers and premium/discount drivers (growth, margins, returns on capital)
Never normalizes for non-recurring items, stock comp, or leases, or fails to calendarize to a common period
Presents a single precise number instead of a range and never reconciles against a DCF or precedent transactions
Confuses trading comps with precedent transactions — misses that transaction multiples include a control premium
follow_ups: Your comps say the company is worth 15% more than a DCF does — which do you trust, and how do you explain the gap?
A peer just got a takeover bid and its stock jumped 30% — do you keep it in the set, and how does that affect your median?
Two peers have very different leverage — how does that change whether you lean on EV/EBITDA or P/E?
The target has a much higher growth rate than its peers — how would you adjust the applied multiple, and would a PEG-type view help?
How would trading comps differ from precedent-transaction comps for the same company, and when would you use each?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong candidate frames comps as relative valuation: 'I'm pricing the target off how the market values genuinely similar public companies, so I'll end with a range, not a point.' They build a tight peer set screened on business model, size, growth, margins, and geography — naming why each company is in or out rather than dumping the whole sector. They choose EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple because it's capital-structure-neutral and normalizes for D&A and leverage differences, noting P/E would be distorted here by different debt loads and tax positions, and they'd use forward multiples for comparability. On mechanics they build enterprise value carefully — diluted market cap via treasury-stock method plus debt, preferred, and minorities, minus cash — and they insist the numerator matches the denominator: EV over EBITDA, never net income under EV. They calendarize peers to a common period and normalize both the metrics and the multiples, stripping a one-time gain out of a peer's EBITDA and flagging a name inflated by takeover speculation. Rather than apply the raw mean, they use the median and reason about dispersion: a peer at 11x is there because it grows faster with fatter margins, so they nudge the applied multiple toward the target's own growth/margin profile — say ~9.0x. Applying 9.0x to $200M EBITDA gives $1,800M enterprise value; less $300M net debt is $1,500M equity value, divided by diluted shares for per-share, and they present the implied range from the 7.5x-11x spread. Finally they reconcile: comps capture current market sentiment and can be collectively mispriced, so they cross-check against a DCF (intrinsic) and precedent transactions (which embed a control premium), and they explain any gap rather than declaring a single 'right' number.

interviewer_notes: This is a mechanics-and-judgment relative-valuation question; the mid bar is a clean, defensible trading-comps analysis plus the judgment to normalize thoughtfully and reconcile against intrinsic value. Let the candidate lay out the framework, then interrupt to test depth: how they actually screen peers (not just by industry code), why EV/EBITDA over P/E, and the precise enterprise-value build — the EV bridge and numerator/denominator matching are where mid-level candidates most often slip. If they're strong, hand them the round numbers in the scenario and make them carry an implied enterprise value, equity value, and per-share figure, then throw in a distorted peer (one-time gain or takeover pop) to see if they normalize or blindly average. The two most common failures are botching enterprise value / metric matching and mechanically applying the group mean without adjusting for growth and margins. Reserve the end for the reconciliation probe — comps vs DCF disagreeing — and reward candidates who present a range, use the median, and can explain why market sentiment and intrinsic value diverge.
